rows.walkScript: Smallest numbers want the smallest digits at the front. But a number cannot begin with zero. So lead with 4, then 0, 0, 7, making 4,007. The trap lets zero lead or loses a placeholder.

stem.text: Round 4,362 to the nearest 100.

options.tagChildHint: Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.
Check which place the question asks for. Then look at the digit after it.
Look at the next digit along. If it is 5 or more, round up.

rows.walkScript: Rounding to the nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. It is 6, so round the hundreds up. 4,362 becomes 4,400. Watch for rounding to another place, or always down.

stem.text: Which of these decimals is the largest: 0.6, 0.55, 0.4 or 0.049?

options.tagChildHint: The decimal point separates wholes from parts. Read each digit after the point in its own column, not as one whole number.
Look at the tenths column first. Which number has more tenths?
Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?

rows.walkScript: Give every decimal the same number of places first. Then 0.60 beats 0.55, 0.40 and 0.049. So 0.6 is the largest. The trap counts the digits after the point as whole numbers.

stem.text: A recipe for 3 people uses 240 g of pasta. How much pasta is needed for 5 people?

options.tagChildHint: Find the cost of just one first. Then multiply that.
Recipes scale up by multiplication. If you double the eggs, you need to double the cakes too.
Count the groups or steps again before you work it out. Use the exact number, not one more or one fewer.

rows.walkScript: Buy the relationship first: the pasta for one person. Share 240 g by 3 to get 80 g each. Five people need 80 g times 5, which is 400 g. A trap adds the extra people or scales by adding.

stem.text: Shop A sells 5 apples for £1.50. Shop B sells 6 apples for £1.20. How much cheaper is one apple at Shop B than at Shop A?

options.tagChildHint: The packs hold different amounts. Find the price of one first.
The packs hold different amounts. Find the price of one first.
Find the cost of just one first. Then multiply that.

rows.walkScript: Put both shops in the same form: the price of one apple. Shop A is 150 shared by 5, so 30p each. Shop B is 120 shared by 6, so 20p each. Shop B saves 10p an apple; a trap compares the packs.

stem.text: A bar chart shows cakes sold: Monday 9, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 7. How many more cakes were sold on Monday and Wednesday together than on Tuesday?

options.tagChildHint: Double-check the chart. Have you added together every single row or bar you need?
Look at the axis labels. Are you counting the right things?
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.

rows.walkScript: Two moves: first add the two days, then compare. Monday and Wednesday together make 9 plus 7, or 16. Take Tuesday's 8 away to leave 8. A trap forgets a day or adds a different pair.

stem.text: The mean of five numbers is 7. Four of the numbers are 4, 9, 8 and 5. What is the fifth number?

options.tagChildHint: Work backwards. Multiply the mean by the total number of items to find your grand total.
Count how many numbers you added. Divide by that.
The mean is an average. Your final answer can be a decimal or a brand new number.

rows.walkScript: Work back from the total. Five numbers with a mean of 7 must add to 35. The four you have add to 26. So the fifth number is 35 minus 26, which is 9.

stem.text: Work out 356 + 287.

options.tagChildHint: Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.
Line the digits up in their columns. Every digit needs a place.

rows.walkScript: Line up the columns and add from the right. Six plus seven makes 13, so carry the ten. Keep going carefully to reach 643. The trap rounds too soon or loses a digit.

stem.text: Work out 483 - 176.

options.tagChildHint: Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
Line the digits up in their columns. Every digit needs a place.
If the top column does not have enough, you need to exchange from the next one.

rows.walkScript: Set the tens and ones under each other. Borrow a ten when the top digit is smaller. Work through to get 307. The classic slip takes each smaller digit from the larger.

stem.text: Work out 43 x 5.

options.tagChildHint: Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.

rows.walkScript: Multiply the ones first, then the tens. Three times five is 15, so carry the ten. Then four times five is 20, plus the carry, giving 215. Watch for a dropped carry or a forgotten tens part.

stem.text: Tom buys a game for £8.75 and a case for £3.60. He pays with a £20 note. How much change does he get?

options.tagChildHint: Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: First add the two prices to find the total spent. That comes to £12.35. Take it from £20 to leave £7.65. The catch rounds the prices or subtracts only one item.

stem.text: Work out 316 x 4.

options.tagChildHint: Write your carried numbers clearly. Then add them to the next column.
Line the digits up in their columns. Every digit needs a place.
Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.

rows.walkScript: Work through the ones, then tens, then hundreds. Six times four is 24, so carry the two. Add each carry as you move left to reach 1,264. A slip drops a carry or loses the hundreds digit.

stem.text: A teacher shares 74 pencils equally between 3 tables. How many whole pencils does each table get?

options.tagChildHint: Leftovers matter! If a column does not divide perfectly, carry the remainder to the next digit.
A remainder is what is left over, but a decimal is a specific fraction. Try writing your remainder as a fraction instead.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: Share 74 pencils equally into three groups. Three goes into seven twice, with one ten left over. Carry it on to reach 24 whole pencils each. The trap splits each digit alone or writes the remainder as a decimal.

stem.text: A club buys 3 footballs at £6.50 each and 2 water bottles at £2.25 each. What is the total cost?

options.tagChildHint: List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
Count the groups or steps again before you work it out. Use the exact number, not one more or one fewer.
Always line up the decimal points. Add place-holder zeros so the columns match perfectly.

rows.walkScript: Work out each set of items before adding. Three footballs cost £19.50; two bottles cost £4.50. Together that makes £24. One slip rounds the prices or leaves a set out.

stem.text: A theatre sells 320 tickets at £15 each. The show costs £1,200 to put on. What is the profit?

options.tagChildHint: List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
You are multiplying by a ten, not a one! What needs to go in the ones column to show this?
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: Find the total money taken before anything else. 320 tickets at £15 make £4,800. Take the £1,200 of costs to leave £3,600. The trap adds the costs or loses a digit.

stem.text: Which is the bigger fraction, 4/7 or 4/9?

options.tagChildHint: The bottom number tells you how many slices the cake is cut into. If you cut it into more slices, what happens to the size of each slice?
You cannot compare them fairly until they are speaking the same language. Make the bottom numbers match first.
Any two fractions can be compared. Draw each one and see which covers more.

rows.walkScript: Common form first: give both fractions the same bottom number. Then 4/7 is 36/63 and 4/9 is 28/63. So 4/7 is the bigger share. The trap thinks a bigger bottom means a bigger fraction.

stem.text: What is 3/4 of 24?

options.tagChildHint: A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.
A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.
Check which number is on top. Turning it over changes the fraction.

rows.walkScript: To find three quarters, first find one quarter. 24 shared by 4 is 6 for one part. Three parts make 6 times 3, which is 18. A common slip stops at one part or flips the fraction.

stem.text: What is 25% of £44?

options.tagChildHint: 50% is a half. 25% is exactly half of that, which makes it one quarter!
Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!
This answer treats the percentage as a whole number. A percentage is a share out of one hundred.

rows.walkScript: 25% means one quarter. Find a quarter of 44 by sharing into four. That gives £11. The catch takes 25 off, halves instead, or rounds the amount first.

stem.text: A hoodie costs £45. In a sale it is reduced by 20%. What is the new price?

options.tagChildHint: You found the discount, well done! Now subtract it from the starting price to finish.
Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!
Percent means "out of 100". To turn a decimal into a percentage, you need to multiply it by 100.

rows.walkScript: First find 20% of £45. A fifth of 45 is £9. Take the £9 off to get £36. One slip stops at the discount or subtracts £20.

stem.text: Which is the bigger fraction, 7/8 or 7/10?

options.tagChildHint: The bottom number tells you how many slices the cake is cut into. If you cut it into more slices, what happens to the size of each slice?
You cannot compare them fairly until they are speaking the same language. Make the bottom numbers match first.
Any two fractions can be compared. Draw each one and see which covers more.

rows.walkScript: Common form first: give both fractions the same bottom number. Then 7/8 is 35/40 and 7/10 is 28/40. So 7/8 is the bigger share. The trap picks the bigger bottom or says they cannot be compared.

stem.text: A car park holds 60 cars. 1/4 of them are red. 2/3 of the rest are blue. How many cars are blue?

options.tagChildHint: Are you finding a fraction of the total, or of what is left?
A fraction is two numbers working together. Use both.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.

rows.walkScript: Name the groups first. A quarter of 60 are red, which is 15. The other 45 are the rest, and two thirds of them is 30. A slip uses the whole 60, or forgets the last step.

stem.text: A coat costs £80. It has 25% off in a sale. Priya also has a £5 voucher. What is the final price?

options.tagChildHint: List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!
You found the discount, well done! Now subtract it from the starting price to finish.

rows.walkScript: Take the steps in order. First 25% off £80 is £20 off, leaving £60. Then take the £5 voucher to reach £55. One slip forgets a step or reads 25% as £25.

stem.text: Two angles sit together on a straight line. One angle is 118°. What is the size of the other angle?

options.tagChildHint: First ask what the angles make: a straight line, a triangle or a full turn. A line and a triangle both make 180°, and a full turn makes 360°.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
If the top column does not have enough, you need to exchange from the next one.

rows.walkScript: Angles on a straight line always add to 180°. Take the known 118° away from 180°. The angle left is 62°. One trap uses a full turn instead.

stem.text: A counter starts at (2, 1). It is moved 5 squares right and 3 squares up. What are the coordinates of the counter now?

options.tagChildHint: Go along the corridor (x) before you go up the stairs (y).
Do not count the point you start on. Each jump to the next grid line counts as one square.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: A translation slides the counter without turning it. Add 5 to the across number and 3 to the up number. The counter lands at (7, 4). One trap reads up before across.

stem.text: In a triangle two of the angles are 30° and 40°. A straight line splits the third angle into two equal parts. How big is each part?

options.tagChildHint: Say the steps out loud in order. Then do them one at a time.
First ask what the angles make: a straight line, a triangle or a full turn. A line and a triangle both make 180°, and a full turn makes 360°.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.

rows.walkScript: The three angles in a triangle add to 180°. Take away 30° and 40° to leave 110°. Split that 110° into two equal parts of 55°. One trap stops before the splitting step.

stem.text: An L-shape is made from a 15 cm by 9 cm rectangle. A 6 cm by 7 cm rectangle is cut from one corner. What is the area of the L-shape?

options.tagChildHint: Find the area of the whole block first, then subtract the piece that was cut away.
Perimeter is the fence around the outside (add the sides). Area is the grass inside (multiply the length by the width).
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: Get the two areas first. The whole rectangle is 135 cm² and the cut-out is 42 cm². Take the cut-out away to leave 93 cm². One trap forgets the cut-out altogether.

stem.text: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm and a length of 9 cm. Work out the width, then the area.

options.tagChildHint: Are you finding a fraction of the total, or of what is left?
You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

rows.walkScript: Halve the perimeter to get 15, which is the length plus the width. Take the 9 cm length off to get a 6 cm width. The area is 9 times 6, which is 54 cm². One trap adds 9 and 6 instead of multiplying. Another uses 15 as the width.

stem.text: A quadrilateral has two angles of 80° and 110°. The other two angles are equal to each other. What is the size of each equal angle?

options.tagChildHint: Say the steps out loud in order. Then do them one at a time.
List every number the question gives you. Check you have used each one.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.

rows.walkScript: The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°. Take away 80° and 110° to leave 170°. Those last two angles match, so halve 170° to get 85°. One trap stops before the halving step.

stem.text: Ben has £8. He buys a toy for £5.60. How much change does he get?

options.tagChildHint: Always line up the decimal points. Add place-holder zeros so the columns match perfectly.
Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
Words like "change" or "left" usually mean subtraction. Take the amount away instead of adding.

rows.walkScript: Change means the totals must line up. Write £8 as £8.00, then take £5.60 away. That leaves £2.40. One trap drops the pence.

stem.text: A plank is 75 cm long. Dan saws off 28 cm. How many cm are left?

options.tagChildHint: Always take the bottom digit from the top. If the top is smaller, exchange.
Words like "change" or "left" usually mean subtraction. Take the amount away instead of adding.
Count the groups or steps again before you work it out. Use the exact number, not one more or one fewer.

rows.walkScript: This is a take-away. Start at 75 cm, the whole length. Cut off 28 cm to leave 47 cm. The trap adds instead, or rounds the 28.

stem.text: Change 6 kg into grams.

options.tagChildHint: "Kilo" always means one thousand. There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram.
Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left. The decimal point does not move.
Check your columns. Hundreds, tens, and ones should only take up three spaces, not four.

rows.walkScript: Name the relationship first: 1 kg is 1000 g. So 6 kg is 6 times 1000. That makes 6000 g. The trap uses too many or too few zeros.

stem.text: A night bus leaves at 23:50. The journey takes 30 minutes. What time does it arrive?

options.tagChildHint: There are only 60 minutes in an hour. Once you hit 60, you need to roll over into the next hour.
In the 24-hour clock, the day starts at exactly 00:00 (midnight).
Count the groups or steps again before you work it out. Use the exact number, not one more or one fewer.

rows.walkScript: Time runs in sixties, not hundreds. From 23:50, ten minutes reaches midnight, 00:00. Twenty minutes more gives 00:20. The trap counts 100 minutes in an hour, or mislabels midnight.

stem.text: Sam buys a comic for £2.65 and a pen for £1.75. He pays with a £10 note. How much change does he get?

options.tagChildHint: You found part of it. Now read the question again and finish.
Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: Get the total spent first. £2.65 plus £1.75 is £4.40. Take that from £10 to leave £5.60. One trap rounds the prices. Another carries a 1 twice.

stem.text: A path is being laid. On Monday 340 m is laid and on Tuesday 275 m. The whole path is 900 m. How many metres are left to lay?

options.tagChildHint: Cross out your carried number once you add it. This stops you from counting it again.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.
Rounding helps you check an answer. Work the real numbers out too.

rows.walkScript: Find the total laid first. 340 m plus 275 m is 615 m. Take that from 900 m to leave 285 m. One trap rounds 275 m and never puts the difference back. Another carries a 1 twice.
